summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk for a trans visitor to the United States. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 requires federal identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth, and new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to the supporting documents submitted; passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records, and the Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to proceed with its changed treatment of trans passports.

Entry carries a second, distinct exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025, titled 'Keeping Men Out of Women's Sports', was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement that trans athletes seeking to enter the United States to compete in women's sporting events will be refused visas, with applicants flagged internally under the code 'SWS25'. The same announcement states that an applicant who declares a gender other than sex assigned at birth may be treated as fraud and barred permanently.

Checkpoint screening risks involuntary disclosure. The National Center for Transgender Equality's know-your-rights guide describes secondary screening, body scanners and pat-downs as procedures that can expose a traveller's trans status to TSA officers and other passengers, and sets out how to request a screening of the type matching one's presentation.

At state level, identity documents are the fastest-moving area of restriction. Kansas has enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licences that do not bear sex assigned at birth and barring trans residents from changing those markers; rights groups describe the Kansas statute as a template other legislatures are following, with further targeting bills pending. The Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map sets out, state by state, which jurisdictions permit gender-marker changes on licences and birth certificates and under what conditions, so the rules a resident or visitor encounters depend heavily on the state involved.

Facility use is regulated in a substantial number of states. State bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings are in force in nine states and one territory, with additional states imposing outright bans on facility use according to gender identity; in some jurisdictions trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances. Twenty-nine states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban. Enforcement is no longer theoretical: in April 2025 a trans student who announced 'I am here to break the law' and used a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol was arrested and handcuffed, in what civil-rights attorneys identified as the first known arrest under a state bathroom-restriction law.

Foreign governments have responded publicly. Following the federal document and data rules, multiple countries issued advisories warning their trans citizens about travelling to the United States. At least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country, and those advisories followed detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Assessments of internal risk are similarly stark. A national legal risk assessment dated 13 July 2026 identifies Idaho as the latest state flagged do-not-travel for trans people, bringing the total to four states so designated, and records that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights alongside the federal measures driving nationwide trends.
tangentialFactors:
The federal measures form a wider package. Executive Order 14168 also defines sex as binary and addresses sex-segregated facilities and care funding; Executive Order 14183 imposes a military ban, Executive Order 14187 restricts care for minors, Executive Order 14190 concerns schools, and a January 2025 federal funding freeze accompanied them. Several of these orders have been blocked or enjoined in court, so the operative position at any given moment depends on pending litigation rather than on the text of the orders alone.

The contest has broadened beyond the areas it was previously known for. Reporting from March 2026 describes the dispute entering a new phase in which bathroom restrictions, limits on health care and document rules are being pursued across states, with Kansas among the principal battlegrounds.

Comparatively, the United States has no national sodomy law and its safety profile varies sharply by state, which is why national figures and single-state examples diverge. Travel guidance for LGBTQ+ visitors accordingly advises checking recent violence reports for the specific destination before departure, since the national picture does not indicate what a traveller will encounter locally.
localsOnly:
Resident document rules are set state by state, and the Movement Advancement Project's identity-document map records which states allow gender-marker changes on driver's licences and birth certificates, by what procedure and under what conditions. Kansas now sits at the restrictive end: its law prevents trans residents from changing markers on birth certificates and licences and treats documents that do not match sex assigned at birth as invalid.

Residents also face the facility rules in force where they live. Nine states and one territory bar trans people from facilities corresponding to their gender identity in K-12 schools and some government buildings, additional states impose broader bans, and some make trans facility use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. The April 2025 arrest at the Florida state capitol indicates that these provisions are being enforced.

Domestic policy exposure extends to health care and funding. Care for minors is restricted under Executive Order 14187, care funding was halted under Executive Order 14168 with a federal funding freeze in January 2025, and trans people are barred from military service under Executive Order 14183. Several of these measures have been challenged and blocked or enjoined in court, and more targeting bills remain pending in state legislatures, so the position for residents continues to shift through litigation.
outOfScopeNotes:
The scale of document refusals is unresolved here. Reports of passports confiscated or blocked at application and of travellers stranded abroad come from individual accounts and press reporting; the inventory supplies no count of affected applicants, no figure for 'SWS25' visa denials and no total for permanent fraud-based bans, so the frequency of these outcomes cannot be stated.

The current litigation status of the passport policy is not fully resolved in the sources. The ACLU suit on behalf of seven plaintiffs, the general court challenge to the X-marker elimination and the Supreme Court's recent allowance of the State Department's changed treatment are all recorded, but the precise injunction posture at the time of reading requires checking against the docket.

Facility-ban counts and document-rule maps are drawn from Equality Map snapshots whose dates are not specified in the inventory, and the 'four states do-not-travel' figure comes from a single advocacy assessment dated 13 July 2026. Both should be verified against current map data before being relied on. Whether other states will follow the Kansas template, and how many of the pending bills will be enacted, is not established by these sources.
